texts.facts: Accused persons CC No. 270/02 Page 1 of 12 JUDGMENT: 1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules. The accused no.1 (since expired) is stated to be the vendor-cum-partner of accused no. 4 firm M/s. Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Laxmi Narain on 18 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153914417/ 1 Kanwarji Bhagirath Mal, of which accused no. 2 and 3 were also the partners, from where the food article, that is, 'Laddu' was lifted for sampling. 2. As per the complaint, on 07.11.2001, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) Arun Kumar and Sanjeev Gupta under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Arun Mishra reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Kanwarji Bhagirath Mal, at 1972, Chandni Chowk, Delhi, where the accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Laddus from the vendor, to which he had agreed. The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules. Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc. The price of sample was paid to the vendor. Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA. Vide report dated 15.11.2001, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that total dye content of the synthetic colour used was 503.45 ppm which was exceeding the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm. Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI. It was revealed that the accused no. 4 was a partnership firm of which accused no. 1,2 and 3 were the partners in charge of and responsible to the firm for its business. After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court on 13.12.2002 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(j) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act. 3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 13.12.2002. The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL). The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL. The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 28.02.2003, opining the sample to be not conforming to the PFA Rues due to presence of dye content upto 670.5 ppm which is more than the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm as per Rule 30 of PFA Rules. 4. The matter was listed for pre-charge evidence wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI Virender Singh and PW-2 FI Arun Kumar. Based on their deposition, vide order dated 05.12.2009 (the charge mentions the date as 04.12.2009), charge was framed against accused no. 2,3 and 4 (accused no. 1 having already expired) for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a),(b)(j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Subsequently, the witnesses already examined in pre-charge stage were recalled for further cross examination in post charge stage and additionally, the complainant examined PW-3 Sh. Arun Mishra and PW-4 FI Sanjeev Kumar Gupta in post charge evidence. It is to be noted that accused no. 1 and 2 have already expired and vide order dated 16.02.2004, accused no. 4 firm has already been discharged. Thus, the trial in this case has been faced only by accused no.3. Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Laxmi Narain on 18 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153914417/ 2 5. PW-2, PW-3 and PW-4 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings. All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 07.11.2001 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Laddus, breaking the same into smallest pieces with the help of clean and dry spoon in a clean and dry tray and then mixing/homogenizing it, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, putting 40 drops of formalin in each bottle, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses. They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-2/A, notice Ex. PW-2/B, Panchnama Ex. PW- 2/C, PA Receipt Ex. PW-2/D and LHA receipt Ex. PW-2/E. PA report Ex. PW-2/F was received and investigation was carried out by PW-2 who sent letter Ex. PW-2/G and Ex. PW-2/H to the STO and Vendor respectively and received their replies. After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/A was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/B was filed in the court by PW-1. A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/C was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/D. These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated. 6. Statement of the accused no. 3 under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 05.06.2013 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence. He stated that he had no knowledge about the sampling proceedings as he was not present at the spot at that time. He further claimed that he was not incharge or responsible to the firm for its business. He chose not to lead evidence in defence.
texts.arguments: 7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused no.3 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 28.02.2003 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive. It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony. 8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses. Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore, conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report. He has relied upon the various judgements in his support. He further submits that there is nothing on record to show that accused no. 3 was the person incharge of or responsible to the firm for conduct of its business affairs. It is argued that when the firm itself has been discharged, none of its partners could be prosecuted under vicarious liability. However, the law has been now settled by the authoritative judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India titled as Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels and Travels Pvt. Ltd. [(2012) 5 SCC 661]. In the said precedent , with pertains to the interpretation of section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (NI Act), Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that commission of offence by the company is an express condition precedent to attract the vicarious liability of other persons and therefore, it is absolutely clear that only when a company can be prosecuted that the persons mentioned in other categories could be held vicariously liable for the offence committed by the company. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India overruled the previous judgements titled as Sheoratan Agarwal v. State of Madhya Pradash [(1984) 4 SCC 352] and Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. [(2000) 1 SCC 1] and reiterated the law as laid down in State of Madras v. C.V. Parekh [(1970) 3 SCC 491]. Reliance can be placed on the judgement titled as SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla [(2005) 8 SCC 89] that pertains to NI Act, as well as the judgements titled as Raghav Gupta v. Food Inspector [Crl. MC No. 1488/2011, Delhi High Court, dated 30.01.2012] and Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Kishan Rohtagi [(1983) 1 SCC 1] that pertain to PFA Act. It has been laid down that that mere averment that an accused being director or partner would 'as such' be liable for the acts of the company/firm would not be sufficient. The judgments relied upon by the accused, that is, State of Haryana v. Brij Lal Mittal [1998 AIPFA Journal 269], MCD v. Kishan Chand [1975 PFA Cases 347], MCD v. Des Raj [1984(II) PFA Cases 163], Chander Bhan v. State [1975 PFA Cases 77], and State v. Naresh Kumar [1980(II) PFA Cases 3] also go in his favour.
